21.22.3.en: For this reason God surrounded the tongue with a double wall, a barrier of teeth and a fence of lips, so that it would not speak easily and hasten to utter words that may not be spoken.

21.23.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The puffed-up, proud man—his name is “scorner,” one who acts in an overflow of pride [24].

21.23.1.en: The wise man sees the haughty man, in the arrogance of his pride, drowning in a destructive flood; the waves of pride toss him about while he does not know it. He is an object of mockery and scorn.

21.23.2.en: * There is nothing for you to be proud of, for whoever sinks into the state of pride receives the results given in the text: “Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour is humility.” These words also belong to the text: “Hear ye, and give ear; be not proud: for the Lord hath spoken” (Jer 13:15).

21.23.3.en: Origen * For in pride dwells the one who says: “By my strength and by the wisdom of my mouth I will remove the borders of the nations, and I will seize their strength, and I will shake cities that are inhabited; and I will take hold of the whole world with my hand like a nest, and I will carry it away like eggs that are left, and no one shall escape me or resist my word.” But the Lord God of hosts will send dishonour upon your glory, and upon your honour a burning fire that consumes. And you also said in your mind, I will ascend into heaven, I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will sit upon the high mountain, upon the lofty mountains toward the east; I will ascend above the clouds, I will be like the Most High. Now you shall go down to hell, and to the foundation of the earth. Let us flee from now on from pride, which the Lord hates, and let us love humility of mind, by which all the righteous pleased the Lord, for humility of mind is an offering of great worth, a great honour, a precious success, and an abundant dignity for those who have acquired it, for in it is a striving that cannot be held back and perfect wisdom; for through exaltation of mind the standing of that Pharisee was humbled, and through humility of mind the standing of the tax collector who was with him was raised.

21.24.0.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian The desire of the slothful killeth him; for his hands refuse to labour [25].

21.25.0.en: He coveteth greedily all the day long: but the righteous giveth and spareth not [26].

21.25.1.en: The slothful man is occupied with thoughts and illusions, and his desire is to gather and hoard, even though he loathes work, reckoning idleness to be health for his body and a power to extort from others. But the righteous man imitates God, who works continually, as the Lord Christ Himself said: “My Father worketh hitherto, and I work” (Jn 5:17). The righteous man imitates his Savior, who gives generously. The Apostle says: “Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Phil 2:4-5).

21.25.2.en: * The complete absence of evil belongs to the angels; that evil desires exist at times and at other times do not belongs to human beings; and that evil desires exist continually belongs to the demons. The expression “all the day long” means the day of life. Therefore also “be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long” means all of life.

21.26.0.en: St. Evagrius The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination: how much more, when he bringeth it with a wicked mind? [27].

21.26.1.en: The wicked man has no fellowship with God, neither obeys His commandments nor submits to Him, so God does not accept his sacrifice and worship, because they come from hypocrisy. How much more, then, if he adds deceit to his evil, even in the sacrifice or worship itself! It is an abomination in the eyes of God.

21.27.0.en: A false witness shall perish: but the man that heareth speaketh constantly [28].

21.27.1.en: The wicked man, with a brazen face, pays no regard to the divine commandment and does not care about the laws laid down by society; rather, he walks in the crooked way of evil and does not care. But the upright man finds his delight in the divine commandment and submits willingly to the laws laid down by society, because they support him in his path of uprightness.

21.27.2.en: A false witness may reach his goal, but only for a while, and his destruction is surely coming. But as for him who speaks the truth, though some may oppose his word for a while, he will be heard in the end.

21.27.3.en: The wicked bore false witness against the Lord Christ (Mt 26:59-64; 27:11-14), and the Lord was crucified according to the plan of the chief priests, the scribes and the Pharisees; but the witnesses perished and the falsehood of their testimony was made manifest. The Lord Christ made the good confession in His trials, and no one cared about Him, yet the Lord Christ was glorified, and the preaching of Him reached to the ends of the earth.

21.27.4.en: * There are true martyrs and false martyrs, just as there are true witnesses and false witnesses. But the Scripture says: “A false witness shall not be unpunished” (Prov 19:5). If the false witness will not escape punishment, then the true witness will not be deprived of the crown. Indeed, it is easy to bear witness to the Lord Jesus Christ, and to the truth, because He is God; but to do this (that is, to witness to Him) even unto death is a great work.

21.28.0.en: St. Augustine A wicked man hardeneth his face: but as for the upright, he directeth his way [29].

21.29.0.en: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the Lord [30].

21.29.1.en: No human wisdom, nor understanding, nor counsel stands against God, and as the Apostle Paul says: “For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth” (2 Cor 13:8).

21.29.2.en: Saul of Tarsus thought that he was able to destroy the truth of the Gospel, but at the appointed time he heard the divine voice saying to him: “I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Acts 9:5).

21.29.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) says that Herod thought to plot against Christ, but he failed to find Him, for the Magi were warned in a dream not to return to Herod (Mt 2:7). [Thus Herod was unable to find Jesus, whom he was seeking. Herod is a symbol of all those who seek the Lord in vain, for they will not reach Him.]

21.29.4.en: * Moreover, David asks God for understanding so that he may grasp God’s commandments, although he knew perfectly well that they were written in the book of the Law, and he says: “I am thy servant; give me understanding, that I may know thy testimonies” (Ps 119:125).

21.29.5.en: Certainly David had the understanding granted to him by nature, and he was fully acquainted with the knowledge of God’s commandments kept in the book of the Law, and yet we find him continuing to pray to God to teach him the Law thoroughly; for the understanding he obtained by nature did not suffice for him unless God enlightened his understanding daily, so that he might understand the Law spiritually and know His commandments clearly.

21.29.6.en: The chosen vessel likewise declared this: “For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Phil 2:13). What could be clearer than this, that our good pleasure and the perfection of our work are accomplished in us completely through God? And again: “For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake”; here he declares that our repentance, our faith and our endurance of sufferings are all a gift from God.

21.29.7.en: David also knows this, and so he prays, as Paul did, that this may be granted to him by God’s mercy, saying: “Strengthen, O God, that which thou hast wrought for us” (Ps 68:28), showing that it is not enough only that the beginning of salvation be granted to us as a gift and grace from God, but it must also be completed and perfected by that same compassion and His continual help.

21.29.8.en: For it is not by our free will, but “the Lord looseth the prisoners”; not by our strength, but “the Lord raiseth them that are bowed down”; not by diligence in reading, but “the Lord openeth the eyes of the blind”; it is not we who take care, but “the Lord preserveth the strangers”; it is not we who support, but God “relieveth the fatherless and widow” (Ps 146:7-9).

21.29.9.en: What I say does not mean that we make light of our zeal, our efforts and our diligence as though they were unnecessary, or that we act foolishly; rather, we must know that we cannot strive without God’s help, and that our striving can be of no benefit toward obtaining the great gift of purity unless it is granted to us through divine help and mercy, for “the horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the Lord” (Prov 21:31), and “by strength shall no man prevail” (1 Sam 2:9).

21.29.10.en: We must sing with the blessed David, saying: “My strength and my song,” not by my free will itself, but “he is the Lord, and is become my salvation.”

21.30.0.en: The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the Lord [31].

21.30.1.en: Reliance on God, and confidence that He grants us victory, does not push us to idleness and passivity, but to action, by preparing the horse for the day of battle, while being certain that victory is from the Lord. The prophet David understood this, and sang: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident” (Ps 27:1-3).

21.30.2.en: When Asa, the good man, stood before Zerah the Ethiopian with his enormous army, Asa called upon the Lord his God, and said: “Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O Lord our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude” (2 Chr 14:11).

21.30.3.en: Our victory in our war against the devil and all his forces, and against sin as well as against the evil world, is from the Lord.

21.30.4.en: * You have lost Paradise, but God has given you heaven, to affirm His tenderness, and that He defeats the devil, showing that even if he perfects tens of thousands of plans against the human race, they will not profit him, since God always leads us to a greater honour.

21.30.5.en: You lost Paradise (the Garden of Eden), and God opened heaven to you.

21.30.6.en: You fell under the judgment of toil for a time, and you have been honoured with life eternally.

21.30.7.en: God commands the earth to bring forth thorns and thistles, but the soil of the Spirit brings forth fruit for you. Do you not see that the gain is greater than the loss?

21.30.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * At the moment when we are still in the midst of the battle, fighting and being wounded, we ask ourselves: Who is winning?

21.30.9.en: The winner, brethren, is the one who relies on God, who upholds him as he fights, and does not rely on his own strength. Satan has his experience in war, but if God is with us we shall overcome him.

21.30.10.en: Satan fights by himself; if we try to do the same, he will defeat us. He is a seasoned warrior; therefore it is fitting for us to call upon the Almighty to stand against him.

21.30.11.en: Let the Unconquerable One dwell in you, and you will overcome the one who is accustomed to win. Whom does he overcome? Those whose hearts are empty of God.

21.30.12.en: * God knows your striving and your good will, and He awaits your struggle, supports your weakness, and crowns your victory.

21.30.14.en: Grant me the spirit of kingship, O King of kings!

21.30.15.en: * My heart, my mind and my whole being are in Your hand.

21.30.16.en: Your divine will leads me, and I enjoy the spirit of kingship.

21.30.17.en: * You carry me in Yourself, O Way, so my soul is at peace in You, and You bring me across into the divine embrace.

21.30.18.en: * You grant me Your righteousness, and my life is turned into a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving.

21.30.19.en: Let all arrogance flee from my heart, and let Your humility reign over it.

21.30.20.en: * I no longer desire anything of the things of the world.

21.30.21.en: I possess You, and so I count everything as vapor and refuse.

21.30.22.en: I possess You, O Pearl of great price.

21.30.23.en: * With You I cannot bear injustice or deceit, whatever enticements they offer me.

21.30.24.en: For You are my wealth and my treasure.

21.30.25.en: * Let Your peace dwell in my heart, so that I know nothing but love for all who are around me!

21.30.26.en: I love everyone and honour the one to whom honour is due.

21.30.27.en: I do not rely on myself, but seek the counsel of my fathers.

21.30.28.en: * I find my happiness in giving, for of what is Yours I give to You.

21.30.29.en: I see You in every poor and needy person.

21.30.30.en: I love them and offer them of what You have granted me.

21.30.31.en: I long to give to everyone, not for material gain, nor to obtain honour,

21.30.32.en: but because I see You giving to everyone generously.

21.30.33.en: * May You dwell in my heart by faith, so that error does not dare to steal into it,

21.30.34.en: and no bodily pleasure is able to draw me away.

21.30.35.en: * Become a wall of fire that guards me, O Holy One.

21.30.36.en: Sanctify my body, my soul and my whole being!

21.30.37.en: Grant me the spirit of strength and victory over evil!

21.30.39.en: With You I bear the spirit of kingship, O King of kings!

22.0.0.en: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold [1].

22.0.1.en: By “a good name” is meant here the “name”: not the name that a man’s parents called him on the day of his birth, nor the one he himself changed for one reason or another, but what a man’s name has come to carry of the features of his character that he has become.

22.0.2.en: When we speak of David, we look to him as a person with certain features, whose heart became an icon of the heart of God. His eldest brother despised him, saying: “Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle” (1 Sam 17:28). But since David consecrated his heart and his life to the Lord, he became not only the first righteous king over the people of God, but the Lord Christ was also ascribed to him, and was called the “Son of David.” This is his wealth, better than all wealth and every temporal kingdom.

22.0.3.en: The Apostles and disciples left everything and followed the Lord Christ, and so they obtained loving favour: and the good name of Christ is better than gold and silver. The Apostle Peter prized this grace, saying to the lame man: “Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk” (Acts 3:6).

22.0.4.en: * A good name is better than money, and loving favour is better than heaps of silver. Faith itself strengthens itself; it is a wealth in which there is sufficiency, and more than the possession of riches.

22.0.5.en: There is nothing that the wise person does not possess except what is against virtue, and wherever he goes he finds all things to be his own. The whole world is in his possession, as it serves him as its king.

22.0.6.en: St. Ambrose * If it is said that the majority of us are poor, this is our glory, and not a shame to us.

22.0.7.en: For just as the mind grows feeble through luxury, and is strengthened by management with economy, so whoever is able to be poor and feel no want, and does not covet what others have, is rich in God’s judgment.

22.0.8.en: The poorer man is the one who, though he has much, desires still more...

22.0.9.en: Happy is he who knows how to raise himself above his poverty rather than groan under the weight of wealth. Yet if we think that wealth is useful to us, we ask it from God; and surely He who is the owner of all things can grant us a share. But we prefer to despise wealth rather than touch it.

22.0.10.en: Rather than wealth, we ask for innocence, and we prefer to ask for patience, and we find it better to be good than to be lost.

22.1.0.en: The rich and poor meet together:

22.1.1.en: the Lord is the maker of them all [2].

22.1.2.en: The Holy Bible took care to emphasize that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Acts 17:26). Humanity represents one family, descended from one father and one mother. The Holy Bible affirms that God is the Creator of all humanity, and His care extends to all; He offered salvation for the sake of the whole world, but He left man the freedom of will to be ascribed to God as his Father or to the devil (1 Jn 3:10).

22.1.3.en: God is the Creator of all, but He will not compel anyone to accept sonship to Him, and He says to the ungrateful: “Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do” (Jn 8:44).

22.1.4.en: * “The poor and the rich meet together.” Where do they meet? In this life. This one is born, and that one is born, and their lives pass by; they meet. And who made them? The Lord. Let the rich man help the poor man, and let the poor man test the rich man.

22.1.5.en: * You two meet together, since you walk the whole way together. It is fitting that the poor man not defraud the rich man, and that the rich man not oppress the poor man. The one is in need, the other has abundance, but the Lord is the maker of both. The Lord helps the needy through the one who has, and the one who has is tested through the one who has not.

22.1.6.en: * All of you are journeying on the same road; you are together as companions on the journey. The poor lighten the load on people’s shoulders, but you are weighed down with a heavy load. Take off from yourselves a share of the load that weighs heavily on you.

22.1.7.en: Give something of your burdens to the poor man. By this you and your companion will find rest. The Scripture says: “The rich and poor meet together: the Lord is the maker of them all.” Where do they meet? Is it not in this life? The one wraps himself in costly garments, while the other is in rags. When do they meet? Both were born naked; even the rich man was born poor. Let him ignore that he found (clothing) when he came, and let him ponder what he brought with him at his birth.

22.1.8.en: St. Augustine * We are all equal by nature.

22.1.9.en: * (Humanity was created complete in the beginning.) Each one has authority to govern himself without a master, to lead his life without sorrow or toil; for what does it mean to be led (by the commands of a master over you) but to be enslaved?

22.1.10.en: * It is not nature but (the love of) power that has divided humanity into slaves and masters.

22.1.11.en: * God gave humanity the right of self-determination (it is not for the master to control the life of the slave).

22.1.12.en: * He who submits to you by custom and law is your equal in the dignity of nature.

22.1.13.en: * To divide creation, which by the right of nature ought to practice equality, into slaves and a ruling power, one part commanding and the other submitting, is tyranny and a usurpation of the order that God established.

22.1.14.en: * (Slavery is) a loss of the integrity of the living being.

22.1.15.en: * The state of independence and freedom is a (natural) inclination toward wisdom and a movement of the human will.

22.1.16.en: * The greatest problem of freedom is for a man to be master of himself.

22.2.0.en: 3 A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished. 4 By humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, and honour, and life. 5 Thorns and snares are in the way of the froward: he that doth keep his soul shall be far from them.

22.2.1.en: A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished [3].

22.2.2.en: By nature the righteous man has no greater abilities than the wicked, nor the wise than the fool, but the righteous man sees evil from afar and takes refuge in God, his shelter, and asks that the riches of His grace may work in him. As it is said: “And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land” (Isa 32:2). But the fool passes on without turning to God. Thus the rich man, like the poor man, can both walk in righteousness if they are careful about their salvation, just as they can choose evil by their own will.

22.3.0.en: By humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, and honour, and life [4].

22.3.1.en: When a man is humble and fears God, he draws abundantly from riches, honour and life. For a man’s wealth does not depend on the material things he has inherited, nor does he gain it from them, but on his clinging to God, the source of wealth, and the opening of his heart to Him through humility and the fear of the Lord.

22.3.2.en: * Just as a lamp lights a dark room, so the fear of the Lord, when it pierces the heart of a man, enlightens it, teaching him all the virtues and the commandments of God.

22.3.3.en: One of the Desert Fathers * Where can my heart flee from my heart? Where can I flee from myself?

22.3.4.en: St. Augustine * If our great heavenly Physician has given us medicines and remedies, where was the cause of our ruin found if not in our own sick purpose? Above all, He has given us humility, which drives out all pride and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of the glory of the Son of God (2 Cor 10:5), and He grants us obedience, which “quenches all the fiery darts of the wicked” (Eph 6:16), and the cutting off of our own will in all things for the sake of our neighbor; and composure of heart, and a face that enjoys radiance and joy, and steadiness in bearing...

22.3.5.en: He has given us a love like His own love! For He became a pattern for us. For He “humbled himself, and became obedient,” not merely obedient, but “unto death” (Phil 2:8). And having sacrificed His life for us, He taught us, saying: “Love one another; as I have loved you,” and “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (Jn 13:34-35).

22.3.6.en: * Humility makes a man a dwelling for God! And the evil spirits, together with Satan their leader, are driven far away from this dwelling with their shameful pains, and thereby the man becomes a temple of God, sanctified, enlightened, purified, rich in grace, filled with every sweet fragrance, tenderness and gladness, and the man becomes a God-bearer (Theophoros), or rather becomes a god, according to the saying: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High” (Ps 82:6).

22.3.7.en: St. Barsanuphius * Abba Longinus was asked: “Which is the greatest of all the virtues, Father?” The elder said: [I believe that just as pride is the worst of all evils, so that it cast some down from heaven itself, so humility is surely the greatest of the virtues, for it can raise a man out of the very abyss, even though the sinner himself has become like Satan. And again, the Lord blessed the poor in spirit before all the others He blessed.]

22.3.8.en: Paradise of the Fathers Thorns and snares are in the way of the froward.

22.4.0.en: He that doth keep his soul shall be far from them [5].

22.4.1.en: The way of the rebellious, stubborn man is crooked, and filled with thorns and hidden snares.

22.4.2.en: * How does the wonderful sweetness of Christ’s yoke become bitter, except because of the bitterness of our evil?

22.4.3.en: How does the exceedingly light divine burden become heavy, except because in our stubborn insolence we make light of the Lord by whom we bear His burden, especially since the Holy Scripture itself clearly bears witness to this, saying: “His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins” (Prov 5:22; Wis 11:16).

22.4.4.en: I say that it is clear that we are the ones who make the easy and sound ways of the Lord into wearisome ways, because of the heavy stones of our wicked desires. For in folly we make the royal road a quarry, and we leave the road that the feet of all the saints have trodden, and in which the Lord Himself walked, seeking a road that has no footprints of those who went before us, seeking places filled with thorns; so the enticements of present pleasures blind us, and the wedding garment is torn by the thorns in the darkness... The road has been covered with rods of sins, so that we are not only torn by the sharp thorns of the bramble, but are cast down by the bites of deadly serpents and vipers lurking there. For: “Thorns and snares are in the way of the froward” (Prov 22:5).

22.4.5.en: The Lord says in another place through the prophet: “Because my people hath forgotten me... and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up” (Jer 18:15). And Solomon says: “The way of the slothful man is as an hedge of thorns” (Prov 15:19). Thus, as they go astray from the heavenly royal road, they are unable to reach the city on which we have set our eyes. The book of Ecclesiastes expressed it figuratively, saying of it that it is Jerusalem... (Eccl 10:15). That is, “Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all” (Gal 4:26).

22.4.6.en: But whoever truly leaves this world and takes up the yoke of Christ and learns from Him, and trains himself daily to endure toil, because the Lord is “meek and lowly in heart” (Mt 11:29), remains continually undisturbed by all trials, and for him “all things work together for good” (Rom 8:28). As the prophet says, the words of God are good to him that walketh uprightly (Mic 2:7).

22.4.7.en: Abba Abraham * Let us also consider how Solomon teaches us to write the divine words upon the tables of our hearts (Prov 3:3; 7:3; 22:20), declaring that “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets” (Prov 1:20). By saying “without” he does not mean to speak about streets, but about hearts, that God may enlarge them.

22.4.8.en: Origen * My son, do not be stubbornly persistent. Leave off laughter and the lusts of your belly and keep away from frivolity.

22.5.s.en: 4. Everyone’s care for the upbringing of children

22.5.0.en: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it [6].

22.5.1.en: By saying “in the way he should go” he means the way fitting for him, which God has drawn for him, so that he grows up in his life walking according to the will of God.

22.5.2.en: By saying “in his way,” and not “in the way you choose for him,” he reveals the necessity of taking care that the child be brought up according to his inclinations and gifts, and not according to what the parents want for him. A wise father and a wise mother study seriously what suits their child’s inclinations from every side.

22.5.3.en: By “child” here is meant the believer who receives the new birth in the waters of Baptism, for the matter does not stop at his baptism, but this is the beginning of the spiritual way.

22.5.4.en: * So here too they call a new child the one who has been born again by the washing of regeneration and has been taught and has become innocent, the one who has become fit for the Kingdom of Heaven through this progress along the same way. Therefore the book of Proverbs supplies us with the exercises that convey to us the understanding and the insight for the newborn, who hungers for the genuine rational milk: the understanding of present truths and the insight into the truths to come. For the child learns human matters, and the understanding of the truth is offered to him, so that he may not be enslaved to shameful lusts, nor long for the glory of this empty world. Besides this, the book of Proverbs gives us an understanding of the life to come, and encourages us to believe the written promises.

22.5.5.en: St. Basil the Great * In general, the commandments of all the saints urge us to this by example, as Solomon used Proverbs, saying: “Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding. For I give you good doctrine, forsake ye not my law. For I was my father’s son, tender and only beloved in the sight of my mother” (Prov 4:1). For the righteous father brings up his children well, for he labors to teach others by his upright and virtuous conduct. So that if opposition arises, he is not ashamed to hear this saying: “Thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself?” (Rom 2:21). Rather he is, as it were, a faithful servant, who can save himself and gain others. And as the grace entrusted to him is multiplied, he can hear that saying: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord” (Mt 25:21).

22.6.0.en: 7 The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. 8 He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity: and the rod of his anger shall fail. 9 He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.

22.6.1.en: The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender [7].

22.6.2.en: The Holy Bible calls on the rich man not to rule over the poor, and the creditor not to humiliate the debtor. At the same time it calls us to flee as far as we can from borrowing, as long as this is within our power. “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another” (Rom 13:8).

22.6.3.en: A man’s recourse to God in his distress gives him a kind of inner freedom, and supports him in solving his problems without abasing himself. We often notice in daily life those who find it easy to beg or to borrow, not out of necessity but for the sake of a luxurious, pampered life, so they sell their freedom for the pleasures of the body.

22.7.0.en: He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity: and the rod of his anger shall fail [8].

22.7.1.en: The wise man compares him who sows iniquity with him who sows goodness, for a man reaps of the same kind as he sows. Pharaoh of Egypt sowed iniquity and violence, and thought himself a man of authority, that none could rescue the people of Israel from his hand, but he reaped bitterness and deprivation, and even destruction for himself as well as for his army.

22.7.2.en: “The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness shall be a sure reward” (Prov 11:18); “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting. And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.” (Gal 6:7-10).

22.8.0.en: He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor [9].

22.8.1.en: The good eye, or the love of giving generously, cannot bear to see a person in distress or want, so the man gives of his bread, that is, of his own needs, with a heart full of mercy and tenderness, and God grants him blessing in his life, and opens to him the storehouses of heaven.

22.8.2.en: * It is not enough for us to do good, for our goodness is not recognized before God if we merely do good, but only if we zealously advance in doing it continually.

22.8.3.en: Many begin, and many persevere in some fashion, but afterward they stop, either because of weariness or because they turn aside from the way. He rightly warns them not to be troubled by any means, lest through their anxiety they abandon what they began when they began a good work...

22.8.4.en: The time is short. Life runs swiftly. The end of the world is at the doors. By saying “as we have opportunity” he means as long as we are in this life, or while there is still life in this world... Therefore we must work, and work good, and work good for all without partiality toward persons. It is fitting for us to do nothing but what is good, and good for all. For love edifies (1 Cor 8:2), and it is necessary to love every person. Therefore every good work we practice must be practiced for all.

22.9.0.en: 10 Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease. 11 He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend. 12 The eyes of the Lord preserve knowledge, and he overthroweth the words of the transgressor. 13 The slothful man saith, There is a lion without, I shall be slain in the streets. 14 The mouth of strange women is a deep pit: he that is abhorred of the Lord shall fall therein. 15 Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him. 16 He that oppresseth the poor to increase his riches, and he that giveth to the rich, shall surely come to want.

22.9.1.en: Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease [10].

22.9.2.en: What does he mean by the scorner, if not the one who mocks the commandment of the Lord and despises the upright life in the Lord? Such a scorner acts like corrupt leaven, and corrupts the whole lump. Therefore the Apostle says: “Put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1 Cor 5:11-13).

22.9.3.en: The removal of the wicked for the sake of his discipline is a divine matter, for God drove Adam and Eve out of Paradise for their discipline so that they might enter heaven.

22.9.4.en: The Law was strict in purging the people of such scorners. “If there be found among you, within any of thy gates which the Lord thy God giveth thee, man or woman, that hath wrought wickedness in the sight of the Lord thy God, in transgressing his covenant, and hath gone and served other gods, and worshipped them... thou shalt stone them with stones, till they die” (Deut 17:2-5). But in the New Testament, along with firmness in purifying the Church, such a person is cast out for a time for discipline, for the sake of his repentance and return to her.

22.9.5.en: It is said in an ancient rabbinic proverb: “When the fool leaves the room, it is as if the wise man enters it.”

22.9.6.en: We grieve at the expulsion of a wicked man who persists in his wickedness, but our grief is bitter, and has fellowship with the grief of the angels when a man is cast out of the Kingdom.

22.9.7.en: * If some resist in disobedience, finding fault in their hidden complaints without declaring them, they become by this a cause of strife in the community, and they spoil the authority of the orders given. Such people must be expelled from the community as teachers of disobedience, and strife will go out with them... “Put away from among yourselves that wicked person. A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump” (1 Cor 5:13, 6).

22.9.8.en: St. Basil the Great * I believe, my beloved, that if Adam, when he was in Paradise, had kept that little commandment, a greater honour than he had before would have come upon him; but when he transgressed the Lord’s commandment he was deprived of joy and gladness and was driven out from where he lived. May God make us worthy to keep His commandments.

22.9.9.en: Father Joseph * How great is the grief of the angels when they see a monk cast out of the Kingdom because of his negligence! And how great is the sorrow of the saints when they behold an ascetic who has not been united with Christ the Bridegroom in His chamber because of his pride!

22.10.0.en: St. Hyperechius the Priest He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend [11].

22.10.1.en: If purity or cleanness of heart opens our eyes to see God (Mt 5:8), and to sit with Him as friends who bear the icon of His holiness, then He also grants the pure in heart favor with emperors, despite the opposition of those who envy him.

22.10.2.en: This proverb also reveals what was in Solomon’s heart, for he longs not for friendship with kings and the great, but with the pure in heart. The true believer finds his happiness in friendship with the pure in heart, to share with them their vision of God: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”

22.10.3.en: * The stillness of the monk with purity of heart draws the Holy Spirit to him.

22.10.4.en: St. Hyperechius the Priest * Abide in purity, and the Spirit will become your friend.

22.10.5.en: * Take care, whether with regard to your eyes or your heart, to abide in rest, and perfect purity will surround you, for God loves holiness, and therefore He says: “For I am holy, and I rest among the holy” (Isa 57:15) LXX. And again: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God,” and again: “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord” (Heb 12:14). For we know that if we bring forth fruits, God purifies us. So strive, then, my son, to abide always in holiness, whether with the eyes or the heart, that you may return to your beginning, like the little children of whom God said: “Of such is the kingdom of heaven.”

22.11.0.en: St. Stephen of Thebes The eyes of the Lord preserve knowledge, and he overthroweth the words of the transgressor [12].

22.11.1.en: God is the Truth, and His eyes are on His truth, which He reveals to His beloved, so that they bear a true knowledge of the truth. He also watches over truth and justice, and will not allow the treacherous and those who falsify the truth to prosper to the end. He is long-suffering toward them, but He will surely expose their deceit and falsehood, and restore the truth to its place. Hanani the seer says to Asa: “For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him” (2 Chr 16:9).

22.11.2.en: * The old man is false, but the new man is truth, and truth is the source of good works, and falsehood is death. If the liar, the thief and the slanderer knew that they would finally be exposed and their deeds be exposed, they would never commit sin at all. So it is with adulterers, like the two sons of Eli the priest, Hophni and Phinehas, for they were priests of the Lord, but they did not fear God, and so they perished with all their house. And the man who keeps the memory of evils and clings to them and shuts them up within himself is like one who hides fire in straw.

22.11.3.en: St. Epiphanius, Bishop of Salamis * There is no straight way except the way of our Lord Jesus Christ, for He is the way, the truth and the life.

22.11.4.en: Abba Timothy * The monk ought to speak the word of truth and keep falsehood far from his mouth.

22.11.5.en: St. Hyperechius the Priest * Humility with discernment is the knowledge of the truth. And the knowledge of the truth is the fountain of humility. He who is humble in his heart is humble in his body, and he who is insolent in his body is insolent in his heart, and he who is disturbed in his body is disturbed in his heart, and he who is disturbed in his heart is ignorant in his mind, and he who is ignorant in his mind, his ways are evil, and he whose ways are evil is dead while alive.

22.11.6.en: St. Isaac the Syrian The slothful man saith,

22.12.0.en: There is a lion without, I shall be slain in the streets [13].

22.12.1.en: Because of sloth, a man is besieged by imaginations that kill his vitality, so he sees the problems around him as an immovable mountain, and sees the people around him as ravening lions; therefore he finds it wise to remain quiet in his chamber without work to preserve his life.

22.12.2.en: * Idleness is the beginning of evil deeds, especially for the uninstructed, for when the Jews had no work to occupy them in the wilderness, they went from idleness to the worship of idols. So do not leave the work of your hands, for it is very beneficial and disciplining.

22.12.3.en: * It was reported to me that a slothful man took the Holy Bible in his lap from the seventh hour (that is, one o’clock in the afternoon) until sunset and could not open it at all, as though it were bound with lead. But Abba Anthony did as the angel showed him: at one time he sat practicing his work, at another he rose and persisted in prayer, and at another he sat reading the word of God. He was granted such enlightenment that he said to one of the philosophers of his time: “It is enough for me to contemplate the nature of creatures continually, and to recite the sayings of the Lord until the darkness of night.” To this degree was he united with God, and his night shone like day, as it is said: “Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day” (Ps 139:12).

22.12.4.en: St. Nilus of Sinai * If you fall, do not delay or be slothful, but rise quickly. And if you go astray, hasten to return until you find the straight road, for the straight road is good, and has no windings and does not need a long time, but quickly brings one to the city of peace.

22.12.5.en: Abba Timothy * One of the Fathers told that near him there lived a brother who labored with God, and then negligence and sloth overtook him. After a while he awoke from his negligence and rebuked himself, saying: “O my soul, how long will you be negligent about your salvation? Are you not afraid of God’s judgment, O wretched one, that while you are in this negligence you will be handed over to everlasting torment?” And when he reflected on things like this, he roused himself to the work of God.

22.12.6.en: Paradise of the Fathers The mouth of strange women is a deep pit.

22.13.0.en: He that is abhorred of the Lord shall fall therein [14].

22.13.1.en: By the strange woman is meant the idolatrous woman, for many of the Jews fell into idol worship because of their idolatrous wives, among them Solomon the Wise, for it is said: “For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father. For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites” (1 Kgs 11:4-5).

22.13.2.en: * The mouth of one who speaks evil is a deep pit, lips that sweep along, sloping down for the innocent, but even more steeply for one whose will is evil. The innocent person believes quickly and easily, and so falls quickly (Prov 14:15), but when he falls he rises. But the slanderer falls recklessly by his deeds, from which he will not escape or come out.

22.13.3.en: St. Ambrose * The conduct of the monk must be pure, and he must not be a mockery to wicked women. For the woman who walks with flattery in the midst of houses is an arrow of the tempter.

22.13.4.en: St. Hyperechius the Priest * Abba Gerasimus met a naked woman in the wilderness. When she saw him she hid from him. He wanted to speak to her, and she hid behind a rock and spoke to him. He said to her: “How long have you been in this wilderness?” She said: “Fifty years.” He said to her: “And what was your food?” She said: “The Creator does not lose what He has created.” He said: “And what have you seen in this wilderness?” She said: “I have seen nothing but Christ and His works and His deeds.” He said to her: “In what is salvation found?” She said: “In your leaving what you are in.” He said to her: “And what is that?” She said: “Your being occupied with weeping over your sins is better than your asking a woman about what does not benefit you.” He said to her: “You have spoken truly,” and he made a prostration (metanoia) and departed.

22.13.5.en: Paradise of the Fathers Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child;

22.14.0.en: but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him [15].

22.14.1.en: The wise man asks parents to discipline their children with wisdom and understanding, so that they may not be bound to foolishness. The “rod” does not necessarily mean bodily punishment, but taking a firm stand joined with parental love and clarity of purpose, namely that the child not deviate from the straight way fitting for the children of God. Discipline with wisdom does not provoke the son under discipline to resentment and anger or a sense of injustice, but leads him to discover his follies and to seek wisdom. The wise man says in another place: “A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool” (Prov 17:10).

22.14.2.en: It is noticed that Solomon does not care only about outward behavior, but concentrates his attention on the heart, saying: “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child.” So he seeks the healing of the heart, even if by the rod of correction.

22.14.3.en: * One of the Fathers said: “There is nothing better than this commandment: not to despise any of the brethren, for it is written: ‘Thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him’ (Lev 19:17). If you know that your brother is in error and do not tell him so that he may know his error, his blood will be required at your hands; but if after the rebuke he persists in the sin and remains in it, he dies in his sin. How good is rebuke when it is done with love and humility, and not with reproach and contempt.”
